doc.title: Chris Parker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 5, 2023

title: Microphones on the drumset and Al Schmitt
summary: Parker thinks ten or twelve mics are overkill, praising Al Schmitt's economical placement, and comments on the seduction of technology like Pro Tools.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Do you have an opinion, with all the recording you’ve done, someone comes out and they’ve got, you know ten or twelve microphones on the drum set. Is it overkill? Does it affect the way you play because you kind of know that the reason they have all these microphones is they’re going to fuss around with the balance?

I understand the engineer’s perspective, he wants to have choices — bottom of the snare drum, top of the snare drum, each tom-tom, overhead cymbals. A lot of guys these days want to have the sound from the drummer’s perspective so they balance things left and right so when you listen back to it if you’re a right handed drummer you’re hearing the hi-hat on the right side and the ride cymbal on the left side. Which is fine you know. But I think ten or twelve microphones is overkill as far as I’m concerned. If you have the right microphone and the right distance from the drum you can get a great sound, you know? And I worked with Al Schmidt a couple of times with Tommy LiPuma and he was a master at microphone placement and the right microphone for the right drum. And it wasn’t ten or twelve microphones, it might have been six — one on the bass drum, one on the snare and overhead he would sometimes mic the hi-hat and sometimes didn’t mic the hi-hat, it really depended on the tune. A mic on each tom-tom but sometimes he would reduce it to just one mic between the two toms and one mic on the floor tom or one mic between the two floor toms. It really depended. If it was a ballad you know you could get away with less microphones. So ten or twelve is probably overkill but it gives the engineer the choices. You know he doesn’t have to use them all or he can mix them and match them, a little of this and a little more of that. And I understand not only the need to do it for their ultimate result but technology is very seductive. You know it’s tempting to have all that at your fingertips. Same thing with Pro Tools, to have all that ability to edit and cut and paste makes it amazing what you can do.
